newsitem.title: USA: Study finds lifestyle link to Alzheimer's disease.
newsitem.headline: Study finds lifestyle link to Alzheimer's disease.

text.p: Men of Japanese ancestry who live in Hawaii have higher rates of Alzheimer's disease than similar men in Japan, a study said on Tuesday, raising questions about the role lifestyle and environmental factors play in the crippling disorder.

"Something associated with migration or with exposure to Western environmental factors has led to higher rates of Alzheimer's disease," said Lon White, chief of the National Institute of Aging's Asia-Pacific Office, who directed the study.

Investigators said they looked at data on 3,734 first- and second-generation Japanese-American men living on Oahu who were born between 1900 and 1919. The men have been part of a continuing heart disease study started in 1965.

The report, published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association, found that 5.4 percent of those studied had Alzheimer's disease, a degenerative condition that erases the memory and leaves victims helpless. A similar study of men living in Japan found a 1.5 percent prevalance of the disease, the report said.
The rate of the disease among the men in Hawaii approached that for men of European ancestry living in the United States, the study said.

It has been known that Alzheimer's is more common in the Western world than in the East. In the West, the prevalance ranges from 37 percent to as high as 63 percent among those over age 85. While the way the disease attacks the brain is known, its exact cause is still a mystery.

Two researchers at the University of Washington, commenting on the study in an editorial published in the same issue of the journal, called the Hawaii report a "landmark" that should encourage a search for more leads on whether lifestyle alterations influence onset of the disease.
"The data ... are the best yet available on the question of whether the introduction of a new environment can make a difference in the occurrence of Alzheimer's disease," the editorial said.

The study also found that the risk of developing another catastrophic condition called vascular dementia, caused by a lack of blood flow to the brain that results in small strokes, was not much different among the men living in Hawaii and those in Japan, for reasons that were not clear.
